name: Rolling Shutter Analysis
description: Analyzes rolling shutter distortion patterns — real cameras produce characteristic row-by-row exposure effects absent in AI video.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated video by analyzing whether the footage contains authentic rolling shutter artifacts consistent with real CMOS camera sensors:

1. **Rolling Shutter Effect Characterization**: Real CMOS cameras expose the sensor row-by-row (or column-by-column) rather than all at once. This means the top of each frame is captured slightly earlier than the bottom — with a typical readout time of 15–33 ms for a full frame. When objects move during this readout interval, they appear skewed (vertical lines tilt), stretched, or compressed. The method models the rolling shutter effect as a row-dependent temporal offset: row r is exposed at time t₀ + r × (t_readout / H), where H is the image height and t_readout is the total sensor readout time. The method estimates motion vectors from optical flow and predicts the expected rolling shutter distortion pattern.

2. **Distortion Pattern Validation**: For any moving object or camera pan, the method computes the expected rolling shutter distortion and compares it to the observed distortion. Specifically: (a) wobble frequency — handheld camera footage produces characteristic low-frequency wobble (1–5 Hz) in vertical edges due to hand tremor interacting with rolling shutter, (b) skew direction — all vertical edges must skew in the same direction consistent with the sensor readout direction, (c) skew magnitude — the amount of skew should scale linearly with object velocity (faster motion = more skew). AI-generated video typically produces either no rolling shutter effects (global shutter appearance) or inconsistent distortion that violates the row-dependent timing model.

3. **Flash and Banding Detection**: Another diagnostic rolling shutter artifact occurs with flickering light sources (fluorescent lights at 100–120 Hz, LED panels with PWM). The row-by-row exposure creates horizontal light/dark bands across the frame because different rows are exposed during different phases of the light cycle. The method detects these bands by analyzing row-wise luminance variation and validating that: (a) band frequency matches a plausible flicker source (50 Hz or 60 Hz mains frequency × 2), (b) bands move vertically across frames at a rate consistent with the readout speed, (c) band contrast is uniform across the frame width. AI generators do not simulate light source flicker or rolling shutter banding, so their absence in conditions where they should occur is diagnostic.

4. **Temporal Rolling Shutter Consistency**: Across consecutive frames, rolling shutter distortion must be temporally consistent — if a vertical pole is skewed right in frame t due to leftward camera pan, it remains skewed right in frame t+1 (assuming continued pan). The method tracks the estimated readout direction and timing across the video and flags inconsistencies: sudden changes in implied readout direction, frames with zero distortion interleaved with distorted frames, or distortion magnitude that does not correlate with measured motion. These temporal inconsistencies indicate either frame interpolation, AI generation, or post-processing that removed/added artificial distortion.
parameters:
Sensor readout time: 15–33 ms (typical CMOS)
Row timing model: linear offset t₀ + r × (t_readout / H)
Wobble frequency range: 1–5 Hz
Skew-velocity scaling: linear relationship
Flicker frequencies: 100 Hz or 120 Hz
Band detection: row-wise luminance FFT
Readout direction: top-to-bottom (most sensors)
Minimum motion: > 2 pixels/frame for reliable detection
Analysis window: 30 consecutive frames
Optical flow: Farnebäck dense flow
accuracy: 81–89% accuracy detecting AI-generated video via rolling shutter analysis. Wobble pattern validation achieves AUC of 0.87. Flash banding detection provides F1-score of 0.84 when flickering lights are present. Performance increases significantly for handheld footage with visible rolling shutter effects.
source: Liang, C. K. et al. (2008). Analysis and Compensation of Rolling Shutter Effect. IEEE TIP, 17(8), 1323–1330.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated video through absence of camera sensor artifacts. Authenticating handheld or smartphone-captured video. Forensic analysis of surveillance footage from CMOS cameras. Distinguishing real video from rendered content.
strengths:
• Exploits physical camera sensor behavior that AI generators don't simulate
• Rolling shutter effects provide a camera authenticity fingerprint
• Flash banding provides an additional independent verification signal
• Works particularly well for handheld footage with motion
• Camera-specific readout parameters enable source identification
limitations:
• Global shutter cameras (CCD, high-end cinema) do not produce rolling shutter effects
• Static scenes with no motion produce minimal rolling shutter distortion
• Heavy stabilization or post-processing may remove rolling shutter artifacts
• Some AI generators may eventually learn to simulate rolling shutter
• Low frame rate reduces the temporal consistency analysis window
